flashcards.back: No. They depend on the informal sections, which explain the key concepts.

flashcards.front: The shallow end / deep end image
flashcards.back: Every chapter ends in the deepest part of the pool (technical metaphysics) but starts in the shallowest part Feser can find.
From real change (actualization of potential) → a purely actual actualizer, the Unmoved Mover.
Older Aristotelian arguments used archaic science (heavenly spheres); the essential kernel doesn't depend on that outdated husk.
From composite things → an absolutely simple, noncomposite cause: Plotinus' One.
God has no parts of any kind. Central to classical theism, yet neglected by contemporary theists and atheists alike.
From universals, propositions, possibilities (real, but not in a Platonic third realm) → a divine intellect.
From the real distinction of essence and existence in contingent things → something whose essence is existence, an uncaused cause of existence (from On Being and Essence).
From the principle of sufficient reason → a necessary being explained by its own nature. Departs from Leibniz; Aristotelian-Thomistic interpretation.

flashcards.front: In what sense is the ch. 5 proof NOT rationalist?
flashcards.back: No commitment to innate ideas or the epistemology of Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz; different interpretation of PSR.
Proportionate causality; agere sequitur esse; the Thomist account of analogical language.
Whatever is in an effect must in some way pre-exist in its total cause (formally, virtually, or eminently).
Action follows being: how a thing acts follows from what it is.
The world could not exist for an instant unless God continually sustained it. Creation is ongoing, not a one-time event.
Creatures have real causal power but can exercise it only as God imparts it at each moment they act.
Pantheism, panentheism, occasionalism, deism.
Crucial for whether there could be knowledge of God through special revelation; whether revelation actually occurred is beyond the book's scope.
None of the objections to natural theology succeeds; the most common ones are feeble and overrated.
Conclusion follows with deductive necessity from certain premises whose certainty is shown by metaphysical analysis — not probabilistic, not best-explanation.

flashcards.front: How do you refute a demonstration?
flashcards.back: Show a premise false, the inference invalid, or the argument question-begging — not by proposing a simpler rival hypothesis.

flashcards.front: Are the five proofs design arguments?
flashcards.back: No. They don't appeal to complexity or probability; a pebble or drop of water serves as well as an eye.
Hierarchical: members depend here and now on borrowed power (cup–desk–floor); must have a first member. Linear: chain back in time; could in principle regress infinitely.

flashcards.front: Do the proofs require the universe to have had a beginning?
flashcards.back: No. They grant a possibly beginningless universe; they concern what sustains things in existence now.
God as pure actuality, absolutely simple, subsistent being itself — not a being among beings or a member of a genus.
God as the unique member of the genus “person,” like us minus limitations; not simple. (Davies: Plantinga, Swinburne, Hartshorne.)

flashcards.front: Do classical theists think God is impersonal?
flashcards.back: No. Most attribute intellect and will to God. The difference from personalism is about genus and composition.

flashcards.front: Where does the real debate lie, per the introduction?
flashcards.back: Among theists of different kinds (Jews, Christians, Muslims, Hindus, philosophical theists), beginning where natural theology ends.

flashcards.front: Three replies to “No one can claim a proof since many reject it”
flashcards.back: (1) Critics often attack caricatures; (2) double standard vs. other philosophical arguments; (3) misunderstanding of demonstration — controversy doesn't entail failure.
Any potential that is actualized is actualized by something already actual. Not the claim that everything has a cause.
Something that could have failed to exist; it needs an explanation outside itself, even if it existed forever.
Made up of parts (physical or metaphysical), so it depends at every moment on its parts existing and being combined.
God as that whose essence just is existence: not a being that received existence, but existence itself.
The claim that things persist in existence on their own. Rejected in chapter 6, since anything composite needs a sustaining cause.
Deism: God starts the world, which then runs without him. Classical theism: God causes the world's existence at every moment.
Only God causes anything; creatures are mere occasions. Rejected: by agere sequitur esse, it would imply only God exists.
God keeps things in being, but they act independently of him. Rejected: it collapses toward deism.
Pantheism: God is the world. Panentheism: the world is in God and changes him. Both are ruled out, since God is simple and immutable.
God elevating nature beyond its own powers or suspending a law. Not a “violation” or “intervention,” like a musician improvising on his own score.
Three ways an effect's feature can pre-exist in its cause. The $20 example: a bill in hand, money in the bank, the power to print bills.
Same sense / unrelated senses / related senses that are still literal. Terms apply to God analogically.

flashcards.front: Ontological argument and the five proofs
flashcards.back: None of the five proofs is ontological. Kant's claim that cosmological arguments presuppose the ontological argument fails: Aquinas rejects the latter while accepting the former.

flashcards.front: Is the Aristotelian proof a priori?
flashcards.back: No. We know change occurs through experience, but no experience could overturn that premise, since every experience is itself a change.

flashcards.front: Ockham's razor vs. the five proofs
flashcards.back: Parsimony judges rival hypotheses. The proofs are attempted demonstrations, so “a simpler explanation” is not a refutation.
The proofs need not start from the universe as a whole; an infinite series of sticks, mirrors, or copied books still needs an outside explanation.
Divine eternity means being outside time altogether, not lasting through endless time.
The lack of something a thing's nature calls for (a blind dog, an injured squirrel). What is purely actual has none, so it is perfect.
We know God truly but only loosely. Simplicity rules out understanding him by parts or by genus and difference.
Belief in God by faith alone, without argument. Feser's position is rationalist, not fideist.
It treats God as one member of the class of gods, like treating triangularity as one more triangle.

flashcards.front: Step 3 of the module argument: what does it claim?
flashcards.back: A demonstration is a deduction from certain premises whose certainty is shown by metaphysical analysis (from chapter 7's final section).

flashcards.front: Step 5: what follows about criticizing the proofs?
flashcards.back: To refute one, show a premise false, the logic invalid, or the question begged, not that a rival seems simpler.

flashcards.front: Step 7: why can't science overturn the premises?
flashcards.back: The starting points (change, composition, contingency, and so on) are presupposed by any possible empirical inquiry.

flashcards.front: Step 10: what does the hierarchical-series point imply?
flashcards.back: No beginning of the universe is needed; God is the sustaining cause now (conservation), not a first domino.
Every proof concludes to a cause with no composition; a being in the genus “person” is composite and would need a cause.
If the proofs succeed, atheism is false and the remaining debate is among theists about revelation.
The kernel (change as actualization of potential) doesn't depend on the husk (celestial spheres); science itself presupposes change.
An ad hominem (poisoning the well); motives cut both ways (Nagel); only the arguments' merits matter.

flashcards.front: Objection “Not the God of religion” → reply
flashcards.back: True that the proofs don't establish revealed doctrines, but that is irrelevant; believers affirm the same God less technically, like a layperson's atoms.

flashcards.front: Objection “A first cause isn't God” → reply
flashcards.back: Stage 2 of every proof, plus chapter 6, derives the divine attributes; critics rarely engage these arguments.

flashcards.front: Why the five proofs are not redundant
flashcards.back: Five different starting points converge on one God. Doubting one starting point leaves four others, and the convergence itself strengthens the case.

teachBack:
**Challenge:** Explain to a thoughtful friend who has never studied philosophy — ideally one who assumes arguments for God are about the Big Bang or design — what Feser's book is trying to do, in **five minutes, without notes**.

**You must cover, in your own words:**
1. What natural theology is, and what it does *not* try to establish (specific revealed doctrines).
2. The difference between a demonstration and a probabilistic or design argument — and what a real refutation would have to look like.
3. The cup–desk–floor picture, and why the proofs don't care whether the universe had a beginning.
4. The five starting points and their conclusions, in one sentence each.
5. The two-stage structure, and why Stage 2 answers “a first cause isn't God.”
6. The difference between the God of classical theism and a “very powerful person.”

**Constraints:** Do not use the words “actuality,” “potentiality,” or “per se” until you've explained the idea with an everyday example. Do not mention any specific religion's doctrines except to say the book leaves them open.

**Check yourself:** Afterwards, ask your listener to tell you (a) why “maybe the universe is eternal” doesn't answer the proofs, and (b) why “What caused God?” misfires. If they can't, identify which of your six points was fuzzy and try again. Then write down one objection your listener raised that you couldn't answer, and find where in chapters 1–7 Feser addresses it.
videoPrompt: Audience: curious, intelligent adults with no philosophy background, including skeptics. Create an orientation to Edward Feser's Five Proofs of the Existence of God. Emphasize, in order: (1) natural theology means reasoning about God without appeal to revelation; (2) these proofs aim at strict demonstration, not probabilistic design arguments — so “a simpler explanation might exist” isn't a refutation; (3) they concern what sustains things in existence right now, not a first moment in time — use the cup held up by a desk held up by a floor; (4) a quick roadmap of the five proofs (change, composition, abstract objects, essence/existence, sufficient reason) and chapters 6–7; (5) the two-stage structure; (6) the God of classical theism is not a being among beings. Correct the misconceptions that the proofs depend on the Big Bang or on scientific gaps. Tone: clear, lively, fair to skeptics, confident but not preachy.

readingGuide.beforeYouRead:
The introduction is the shortest and easiest part of the book — about seven pages — and it is mostly a guided tour. It won't ask you to accept any argument yet. Its job is to tell you what kind of book you're holding, what the five arguments will be, and how each chapter is put together.

Here is the big picture. Feser wants to show that you can know God exists by reasoning alone, without relying on the Bible, a church, or personal faith. That project is called **natural theology**. He also claims something bolder than most modern writers on religion: these aren't “best guess” arguments that make God seem likely. They are meant to be **proofs**, in the strong sense that if the starting points are true and each step follows, the conclusion must be true.

Why would anyone care? If Feser is right, the usual debate — “Is there a God or not?” — gets settled, and the interesting question becomes whether God has revealed anything, and which religion (if any) has it right. The book itself doesn't try to answer that second question.

As you read, you'll meet a few names (Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Aquinas, Leibniz) and a few technical-sounding phrases (“purely actual actualizer,” “principle of sufficient reason,” “real distinction between essence and existence”). **Don't worry if these don't make sense yet.** In the introduction they are just labels on the map. Each one gets a full, slow explanation in its own chapter, starting from everyday examples like a cup of coffee cooling on a desk.

What you *should* try to come away with is three things. First, what natural theology is. Second, the fact that every proof comes in two stages: first “there must be something of this kind,” then “and it must be God.” Third, the roadmap of the seven chapters. If you have those, you're ready for chapter 1.

One more reassurance: Feser admits the book gets technical, but he promises to start every chapter “in the shallow end.” The introduction is the shallowest water of all.

knowFirst.plain: Trying to learn about God — whether God exists and what God is like — using reasoning alone, without appealing to scripture or faith.
Knowledge about God that would come from God telling us something directly, for example through prophets or holy books. The book sets this question aside.
A proof in the strong sense: if the starting points are true and every step follows, the conclusion has to be true. It's the opposite of a “probably” argument.
Every proof first shows that something of a certain kind must exist, then shows that this something has to have God's features.
The features traditionally belonging to God: being one, eternal, non-physical, all-powerful, all-knowing, and perfectly good.
The traditional view of God as the source of all existence — not the biggest being in the universe, but existence itself, with no parts at all.
The idea that God isn't made of parts of any kind. “Simple” here means “not put together,” not “easy to understand.”
What a thing actually is versus what it could become. Hot coffee is actually hot and potentially cold; change is a potential becoming actual.
Explaining what an author meant in a text. Feser says this book doesn't do that; it defends arguments directly.

questionsToHold: What exactly is Feser trying to prove, and what does he say he is *not* trying to prove?
Why does Feser think a “proof” of God is possible, when many people assume the best you can get is “probably”?
What do the five starting points (change, having parts, abstract truths, what-a-thing-is versus that-it-is, and the need for explanation) have in common?
Why does each proof need a second stage after it shows that some ultimate cause exists?
If all five arguments work, why would they all lead to the same God rather than five different ones?
What would change about the debate over religion if these arguments succeed?

map.section: Opening (the introduction has no internal headings): not a book about the Five Ways
map.what: Feser says this isn't another book on Aquinas' famous Five Ways. The arguments are old, but most philosophers today ignore them, which he blames on the state of philosophy rather than on the arguments.
map.tip: Read the footnote listing the Five Ways, but don't try to memorize it. Just notice that the book will cover different ground.

map.section: Natural theology and Feser's earlier books
map.what: He defines natural theology (what reason alone can know about God) and explains why his earlier Aquinas books needed long philosophical preliminaries.
map.tip: Slow down on the definition of natural theology. It is the single most important sentence in the introduction.

map.what: The book defends the most important arguments directly, with no textual interpretation and with background ideas introduced only as needed. Two proofs come from Aquinas; three don't.
map.tip: Note the five thinkers (Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Aquinas, Leibniz) and the idea of an argument “inspired by” rather than “taken from” them.

map.section: How each proof chapter is built: the two-stage informal statement
map.what: Each chapter first explains its argument informally in two stages: something of a certain kind exists, then it must have God's attributes. Feser explains why he starts informally.
map.tip: This is the key structural idea of the book. Reread until you can explain Stage 1 and Stage 2 in your own words. Enjoy the swimming-pool image.

map.what: Each chapter then gives a numbered, step-by-step version and ends with a long section answering objections.
map.tip: Remember the warning: the numbered version isn't meant to be read on its own. When you reach chapter 1, read the informal part first.

map.what: From the fact of change to an “Unmoved Mover.” Feser notes that the old versions used outdated astronomy but the core idea doesn't depend on it.
map.tip: Don't worry about “actualization of potential” yet; chapter 1 explains it with coffee and cups. Do notice the kernel-and-husk point about old science.

map.section: Roadmap: chapters 2 and 3, the Neo-Platonic and Augustinian proofs
map.what: Chapter 2 argues from things having parts to a cause with no parts (“the One”); chapter 3 argues from abstract things like numbers and truths to the mind of God.
map.tip: Mark the sentence calling divine simplicity central to the traditional idea of God. It will matter all through the book.

map.what: From the difference between what a thing is and the fact that it exists, to something whose very nature is to exist.
map.tip: This is the most abstract-sounding summary. It's fine to leave it half-understood until chapter 4.

map.what: From the principle that everything has an explanation to a being that exists necessarily. Feser explains in what limited sense the argument is “rationalist.”
map.tip: You can skim the parenthesis about Descartes, Spinoza, and innate ideas on a first read. The point is only that “rationalist” is used narrowly.

map.section: Roadmap: chapter 6, God's nature and relationship to the world
map.what: Three background principles; why all five proofs reach the same God; the list of divine attributes; how God keeps the world in existence and empowers it; which rival views are ruled out; what a miracle is.
map.tip: This is the densest paragraph in the introduction. Read it slowly, and don't expect to understand terms like “concurrence” or “occasionalism” yet — just note that chapter 6 will explain them.

map.section: Roadmap: chapter 7, and the closing “confident discipline” passage
map.what: Chapter 7 answers common objections. Feser then defends his confident tone by pointing to the long tradition behind it, and concludes that if the proofs succeed, the real debate is among different kinds of believers.
map.tip: Read the last paragraph twice. Make sure you can say what the book does not try to settle.

afterReading: Without looking, define natural theology in one sentence, and give one example of a premise it could use and one it couldn't.
Explain Stage 1 and Stage 2 of the proofs to an imaginary friend in under a minute.
List the five proofs in order with their starting points (change, parts, abstract objects, essence versus existence, sufficient reason).
State what chapter 6 and chapter 7 are for, in one sentence each.
Write down what Feser says the book does not try to settle, and why that matters.
Explain why the formal, numbered versions of the arguments shouldn't be read on their own.
Note one claim in the introduction that you find surprising or doubtful, and keep it in mind as you read chapter 1.
